failures.title: BMW S63B44T3 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Cooling system failures - hot‑vee heat management
items.whatHappens: The S63's hot‑vee design (turbochargers mounted in the V of the engine) generates significant heat, placing the cooling system under constant stress. Common failures include coolant leaks from the expansion tank, water pump failure, and cracked coolant hoses around the turbochargers. Coolant loss can lead to overheating and, if ignored, head gasket failure.
items.repairVsReplace: Coolant system components (water pump, expansion tank, hoses) are individually replaceable - usually £500-£1,500 depending on which parts have failed. A full engine replacement is not typically required for cooling issues alone, though overheating can cause additional damage. → Read our full coolant system failure guide

items.title: Turbocharger issues - wastegate rattle / oil supply
items.whatHappens: The twin‑turbochargers on the S63B44T3 can develop wastegate rattle (a metallic noise at low RPM), caused by wear in the wastegate bushings. Oil supply issues to the turbos can also occur if oil changes have been neglected, leading to turbo failure.
items.repairVsReplace: Wastegate rattle can sometimes be addressed with a wastegate repair kit, though full turbo replacement (around £2,000-£4,000 each) is common on higher‑mileage examples.

items.title: Valve stem seals - oil consumption
items.whatHappens: Like many turbocharged BMW V8s, the S63 can develop valve stem seal wear, leading to oil consumption, blue smoke on startup, and fouled spark plugs. This is a labour‑intensive repair as the cylinder heads must be removed.
items.repairVsReplace: Valve stem seal replacement is a substantial job (around £2,000-£4,000) but far cheaper than a full engine replacement. Many owners also address the coolant system and turbo oil lines while the engine is partially dismantled.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the S63B44T3
variants.intro: The S63B44T3 is a specific engine code within the S63 family, representing the third major technical revision (T3) of BMW's 4.4‑litre twin‑turbo V8. The S63 family includes: - S63B44 - original 2009-2013 (M5 F10, X5M/X6M E70/E71) - 555‑560 hp - S63B44T2 - 2013-2018 (M5 F10 LCI, X5M/X6M F15/F16) - 575‑600 hp - S63B44T3 - 2018‑present (M5 F90, M8, X5M/X6M G05/G06) - 592‑625 hp - S63TU - Family page covering multiple S63 variants How to confirm your code: 1. On the engine - the S63B44T3 code is stamped on the engine block. Look for "S63N" or "S63B44T3" on the identification plate on the left‑hand side of the engine. 2. On the V5C logbook - the engine number is listed; cross‑reference with BMW parts systems. 3. VIN decode - use a BMW VIN decoder; F90 M5, F92 M8 and G05/G06 X5M/X6M vehicles show engine type "S63B44T3". 4. Registration lookup - enter your reg above and we'll confirm the exact fitment. Similar‑looking codes it is commonly confused with: - BMW S63B44T2 - the previous generation, fitted to F10 M5 LCI and F15/F16 X5M/X6M; not a direct swap - BMW S63B44 - the original 2009‑2013 version; significant differences in cooling, turbo and ECU - BMW S63TU - Family page covering the S63 evolution

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement S63B44T3 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used S63B44T3 makes sense only if the donor has documented service history with BMW LL‑01 FE oil, low mileage (under 50,000 miles), and evidence that the cooling system and turbo oil lines have been maintained. The primary risk with used units is undisclosed coolant system wear - insist on a pressure test and turbo inspection before purchase. For lower‑value F90 M5 or X5M examples, a used unit with documented history can be a cost‑effective option. View used engines

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper S63B44T3 recon addresses the cooling system (new water pump, expansion tank, hoses), replaces the turbochargers or rebuilds wastegate components, fits new valve stem seals and gaskets, and checks the timing chain tensioners. This is the right call for most replacements - you get a like‑new unit with the known weak points already addressed, backed by 12-24 months warranty. View reconditioned engines

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified for high‑value, collectable or low‑mileage M cars where originality matters. An upgraded rebuild should include upgraded turbochargers, improved cooling system components, and forged internals if tuning is planned. For standard applications, reconditioned is usually more cost‑effective. View rebuilt engines

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: All engines can be supplied and fitted through our network of vetted UK BMW M specialists - nationwide coverage with 12‑month warranty on labour and parts. View supply & fit
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The S63B44T3 sits exclusively in high‑performance M cars - F90 M5 (£25,000-£60,000+), M8 (£40,000-£100,000+), X5M/X6M (£40,000-£80,000+). A £9,000-£14,000 reconditioned engine plus £1,500-£2,500 fitting is a significant but often justifiable investment - typically 20-40% of the vehicle's value. For lower‑value examples (sub‑£25,000 M5s or higher‑mileage X5Ms), carefully evaluate the car's overall condition, service history and specification before committing. For collectable Competition or CS models, the investment is almost always justified given the rarity and value of the car.
